newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Rwanda appeals for $700 mln at Zaire aid meeting.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda appeals for $700 mln at Zaire aid meeting.

text.p: Western aid chiefs, donors and relief agencies met on Saturday to coordinate relief efforts for east Zaire as Rwanda said it would need $700 million to resettle about half a million returning Hutus.

Aid officials said the one-day meeting, chaired by Canada's international cooperation minister Don Boudria, would mobilise support for Rwanda that faces the daunting task of reintegrating the flood of refugees in Africa's most crowded country.
The talks opened as military commanders in Stuttgart, Germany, continued a meeting to discuss an armed intervention force to bring aid to Rwandan and Burundian refugees in Zaire.
The Stuttgart talks were extended amidst confusion over how many people need help, and where they are located.
Canada's Boudria told reporters that the focus of the Geneva meeting was strictly on humanitarian aid.

"We don't intend to do anything here that has anything to do with the military. We have to stick to the focus of humanitarian aid. The great needs are there and everyone's efforts are required," he told reporters.

More than half a million Rwandan Hutus streamed back home earlier this week, fleeing a Tutsi revolt in eastern Zaire where the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR says another 700,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees are still on the run.
Rwandan government delegation chief, transport and telecommunications minister Charles Murigande, said his country urgently needed funds to build new homes for returnees.

"We have made an assessment of needs for speedy resettlement and reintegration of refugees. We need around 700 million dollars. The main elements are emergency need for food and quick assistance. But housing is the major aspect," he told reporters.
"The government of Rwanda will be the beneficiary of whatever decision is taken here," he added.
The returnees were among one million Hutus who fled in fear of retribution of 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis, after which a Tutsi-dominated army swept to power in Rwanda.
The mass return has shifted the thrust of relief efforts to Rwanda, where genocide wounds are still fresh among minority Tutsi survivors and ethnic tensions are dangerously high.
More than 800,000 Tutsis who fled abroad during earlier bouts of ethnic conflict returned to Rwanda after the genocide.

The new Tutsi arrivals, almost a one-to-one replacement of the genocide dead, have settled in abandoned homes of Hutu refugees. Some Tutsis, trying to quash property claims of returning Hutus, have falsely accused Hutus of genocide.

Diplomats say solving the housing crisis is key to reconciliation efforts in Rwanda, where a centuries-old rivalry over farmland has been at the root of much of the animosity between majority Hutus and Tutsis.
"We all worked very hard to get the refugees back to Rwanda and we'll help Rwanda rebuild a country with all its people," U.N. High Commissioner for refugees Sadako Ogata told reporters.
The Geneva meeting is attended by high-level representatives from European donor countries including French state secretary for humanitarian affairs Xavier Emmanuelli.
Also participating are U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) chief Brian Atwood and International Committee of the Red Cross president Cornelio Sommaruga.

Zaire was represented at the meeting by its diplomats based in Geneva. Senior representatives from the government of Zaire, where aid agencies have yet to have access to thousands of refugees on the run, were not invited, Canadian officials said.

The Geneva gathering comes amid growing controversy over how many refugees actually are on the run in eastern Zaire. Complete confusion reigns over the whereabouts and number of the Rwandan refugees and of the many thousands of displaced Zaireans.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril of Canada, which is coordinating the U.N.-authorised mission, told a news conference in Stuttgart that estimates varied between 100,000 and 500,000. These figures are well below UNHCR estimates.
